questions.stem: In film, 'mise-en-scène' refers to:
options: the dialogue written for the actors in the screenplay
everything in the frame: setting, costume, lighting, props and actors
the editing of separate shots into a meaningful sequence on the screen
the musical score composed to accompany the action of the film
questions.explanation: Mise-en-scène, 'placing on stage', covers all that is arranged before the camera. The joining of shots in sequence is editing or montage, a separate element of film form.

questions.stem: In film, a voice-over is:
options: dialogue recorded on set and heard as the characters speak it in the scene
a written caption placed on screen to identify a time or a place
music from a source within the scene, such as a radio or a band
narration heard over the images by a voice not shown speaking
questions.explanation: Voice-over is a common way to carry a novel's narrating voice into film. Music from a radio within the scene is diegetic sound, which belongs to the story world.

questions.stem: A shot that shows exactly what a character sees, so the audience shares their view, is a:
options: two-shot
point-of-view shot
establishing shot
long shot
questions.explanation: A point-of-view shot aligns viewers with a character's perspective, the closest film comes to first-person narration. An establishing shot opens a scene by showing its location.

questions.stem: A film opens with a long shot of a tiny figure walking across a vast, empty desert. The shot most likely emphasises the character's:
options: cruelty and menace
isolation and insignificance
power and control over others
wealth and status
questions.explanation: Dwarfing a figure in a huge landscape makes them seem small and alone. A low-angle shot, rather than a distant one, is the usual way to suggest power.

questions.stem: A film scene is lit with strong shadows and pools of darkness, a style known as low-key lighting. This lighting most often creates:
options: a documentary sense of calm neutrality
the bright clarity of comedy
mystery, menace or moral uncertainty
cheerful warmth and security
questions.explanation: Low-key lighting, central to film noir, hides as much as it shows, suiting stories of danger and divided motives. Comedies and musicals more often use bright, even high-key lighting.

questions.stem: A film alternates repeatedly between a wedding and a robbery taking place at the same time across town. This editing technique is:
options: a montage of years
a long take
cross-cutting
a match cut
questions.explanation: Cross-cutting, or parallel editing, interweaves simultaneous scenes to build suspense or invite comparison. A long take is a single unbroken shot, the opposite of rapid alternation.

questions.stem: A novel spans ten years in a single sentence: 'The seasons turned, and she grew up.' A film is most likely to convey this passage of time through:
options: a single long take that lasts the full ten years of her life
a soliloquy in which she lists the years aloud
a freeze-frame held on her face as a child
a montage of brief shots showing her at different ages
questions.explanation: Montage compresses time by linking a series of short shots, much as the novel's sentence summarises years. A freeze-frame stops time rather than moving it forward.

questions.stem: A film cuts from a spinning roulette wheel to a spinning car wheel as a gambler drives away. This match cut most likely:
options: shows two unrelated events happening at the same time
breaks the fourth wall by addressing the audience directly
links the images to suggest his life is still a gamble
signals a flashback to the gambler's childhood memories
questions.explanation: A match cut joins shots through a similar shape or movement, inviting viewers to connect their meanings. The cut follows the gambler forward in time, so it is not a flashback.

questions.stem: In theatre, an aside is:
options: a brief remark to the audience that other characters do not hear
a long speech delivered by a character standing alone on the stage
a printed instruction to actors about movement and setting
a scene in which a group sings in unison between acts
questions.explanation: An aside shares a quick thought or plan with the audience while other characters are present. A long speech alone on stage is a soliloquy.

questions.stem: The 'fourth wall' in theatre is:
options: the side wings where actors wait to enter
the imaginary barrier between the stage and the audience
the painted backdrop hung at the rear of a realistic stage set
the curtain that falls at the end of each act
questions.explanation: Realistic drama acts as if the audience were watching through an invisible wall, and characters who address the audience directly 'break' it. The backdrop and wings are physical parts of the stage.

questions.stem: A stage adaptation of a war novel has actors hold up placards of casualty figures and speak directly to the audience. These Brechtian techniques most likely aim to:
options: add realism by recreating the novel's battlefield as closely as possible
replace the novel's ideas with spectacle designed purely to entertain
stop the audience losing itself in emotion so it judges the issues critically
make the audience forget it is watching a play and feel part of the war itself
questions.explanation: Brecht's alienation effect deliberately breaks illusion so that audiences think about the social and political causes of what they see. Encouraging the audience to forget it is watching a play is the aim of the realist illusion that Brecht rejected.

questions.stem: A novel contains long passages of a character's private reflection. A stage adaptation is most likely to convey these through:
options: free indirect discourse
a close-up on the actor's face
soliloquy or direct address
a point-of-view shot
questions.explanation: Theatre has no narrator or camera, so characters must speak their thoughts aloud. Close-ups and point-of-view shots belong to film, and free indirect discourse to prose.

questions.stem: A play script's stage direction reads only 'A long pause.' In performance, the meaning of the pause:
options: is fixed by the script, so every production must play it identically
is lost entirely, because audiences never notice silence on stage
must be explained to the audience by a narrator who steps forward
depends on the director's and actors' choices, so productions differ
questions.explanation: A script is completed by performance, and a pause can be played as menace, grief or comedy. This is one reason a staged production is itself a kind of adaptation of the written play.

questions.stem: A stage production darkens the set and isolates one character in a single spotlight. The effect is most likely to:
options: signal that the play's action is moving to an outdoor location
indicate that every character on stage is speaking at once
focus attention on the character and suggest an inner, private moment
show the passing of many years in the space of only a few seconds
questions.explanation: Isolating a figure in light cuts them off from the world of the scene, often marking a soliloquy or a moment of reflection. Lighting can suggest time and place too, but a lone spotlight works mainly by focus.

questions.stem: In a screenplay, a scene heading such as 'INT. KITCHEN – NIGHT' indicates:
options: whether the scene is interior or exterior, its location and its time of day
the camera angle and the lens to be used for the opening shot of each scene
the character who speaks first and the emotion with which they speak
the music to be played under the scene and the volume at which it plays
questions.explanation: Scene headings, or sluglines, tell the production where and when each scene takes place. Camera directions and music are usually left to the director and composer.

questions.stem: 'Fidelity criticism' judges an adaptation mainly by:
options: how closely it reproduces its source text
how much money it earned at the box office
how many awards its actors received
how recently it was released
questions.explanation: Fidelity criticism treats the source as the standard and changes as failures. Many critics argue this misses how adaptations create new meanings in a new form and context.

questions.stem: Linda Hutcheon describes adaptation as 'repetition without replication'. This suggests that an adaptation:
options: must copy its source exactly, or else it is not truly an adaptation
has no real connection with the source on which it is based
always improves on its source by removing what is unnecessary
repeats a source while changing it, and is a work in its own right
questions.explanation: Hutcheon argues that adaptations both recall and transform their sources, so they should be read for what their changes do. Treating any departure as a failure is the fidelity approach she argues against.

questions.stem: Hutcheon argues that audiences who know a source experience the adaptation 'as palimpsests'. This means such viewers:
options: cannot enjoy the adaptation unless it copies the original exactly
read the adaptation as if it were the original text itself
experience the new work alongside their memory of the original
forget the original entirely once they have seen the adaptation
questions.explanation: A palimpsest is a manuscript written over an earlier text that still shows through, so the source shadows each moment of the adaptation for those who know it. This doubled experience is part of adaptation's pleasure and meaning.

questions.stem: In Geoffrey Wagner's three modes of adaptation, a film that departs considerably from its source to make a new work of art, such as by moving it to a very different time and place, is an:
options: transposition
commentary
abridgement
analogy
questions.explanation: Wagner distinguished transposition, which follows the source closely, commentary, which alters it in some respect, and analogy, a considerable departure that makes another work. A near-direct translation to screen would be a transposition.

questions.stem: In Julie Sanders' terms, an appropriation differs from an adaptation in that it typically:
options: is always made in the same form as the original text
moves further from its source into a new cultural product
copies its source more faithfully than any adaptation could
names its source more openly, usually in its title
questions.explanation: Sanders sees adaptation as signalling a clear relationship with its source, while appropriation makes a more decisive move away into something new. The two terms describe a spectrum of closeness rather than fixed categories.

questions.stem: Rather than asking whether an adaptation is 'faithful', a strong comparative analysis asks:
options: how and why the changes create different meanings
which version the analyst personally enjoyed more
whether the adaptation used famous actors
how long each version takes to read or watch
questions.explanation: The study design's focus is on differences in meaning that arise when a text is adapted, so changes are treated as choices to be interpreted. Personal preference is not analysis, however strongly it is argued.

questions.stem: A director sets a Renaissance tragedy about two feuding families in a modern city of rival gangs, with guns in place of swords. This transposition most likely:
options: removes the play's concern with violence by changing its historical setting
proves that the original play was really written about modern gang culture
turns the tragedy into a comedy, because modern settings undercut tragic seriousness
makes the play's concern with cycles of violence immediate for a modern audience
questions.explanation: Updating the setting lets a modern audience recognise the feud in its own world while the play's language and ideas remain. The change reframes the original rather than revealing a hidden modern subject.

questions.stem: A 19th-century novel briefly mentions a servant who never speaks. A modern adaptation gives her a central role and her own perspective. This change most likely:
options: shows that the original novel was mainly concerned with the servant's own point of view
removes the class concerns of the original by focusing closely on a single individual character
keeps the original's meaning unchanged, since the servant was already present in the novel
foregrounds a viewpoint the original marginalises, inviting a critique of its class assumptions
questions.explanation: Giving voice to a silent character brings into view what the original left at its margins and can expose the assumptions that kept her there. Her presence in the novel without a voice is exactly what the adaptation transforms.

questions.stem: A Hollywood film adaptation from the 1940s removes all references to the heroine's affair. The most likely reason is:
options: the director's need to make the film longer than the novel
the censorship rules and moral codes of the film's own context
a wish to make the heroine's story more historically accurate on screen
the novel's affair being too short to film effectively
questions.explanation: Hollywood's Production Code, enforced from 1934, restricted the depiction of adultery and other 'immoral' behaviour. Adaptations bear the marks of the context in which they are made, not only of their source.

questions.stem: A director known for environmental activism adapts a 19th-century novel and adds lingering shots of clear-felled forests. The most valid analytical claim is that the adaptation:
options: keeps exactly the same emphasis as the novel it is adapting
is invalid, because adaptations must not add new material
foregrounds an ecological concern reflecting its creator's viewpoint
proves that the novelist intended the novel as an environmental warning
questions.explanation: Creators' viewpoints shape what an adaptation emphasises, so new images can reorient a text towards their concerns. The adaptation reveals the director's reading, not proof of the novelist's intentions.

questions.stem: A production casts a woman as a ruler who was written as a man. The casting choice is most likely to:
options: leave the play's meaning exactly as it was, because the words themselves are unchanged
prove that the playwright secretly intended the ruler to be a woman
remove all of the play's interest in power and the politics of rule
invite the audience to reconsider the play's assumptions about gender and power
questions.explanation: The same lines spoken by a different body can carry new meanings, so casting is itself an interpretive act. Unchanged words do not guarantee an unchanged meaning in performance.

questions.stem: An adaptation made decades after a novel presents the hero's persistent pursuit of an unwilling woman as harassment, where the novel presented it as romance. This difference shows that:
options: the adapters misread the novel and failed to understand its plot
the adaptation's context and values reshape how the original's ideas appear
the novel itself presented the pursuit as harassment from the very first chapter
adaptations cannot change the meaning of the texts they are based upon
questions.explanation: Changing social attitudes lead adapters to reframe behaviour that the original treated as natural, exposing the original's assumptions. That is a reinterpretation, not a failure to understand the plot.

questions.stem: A novel's meaning depends on a first-person narrator whose thoughts gradually reveal that she is unreliable. A film adaptation without voice-over would most likely convey this through:
options: an omniscient narrator who explains her lies in the final scene
removing her completely so that no viewpoint is unreliable
contradictions between what she says and what the camera shows
a printed caption announcing that she cannot be trusted
questions.explanation: Film can create unreliability by letting images undercut a character's words, so viewers see more than she admits. An explaining narrator would replace the novel's gradual discovery with a plain statement.

questions.stem: An adaptation cuts a novel's ironic narrator and presents the events only through dialogue and action. The most likely difference in meaning is that:
options: the ironic distance guiding readers' judgement is lost or must be rebuilt
the characters become harder to understand because they no longer speak at all
the adaptation becomes more ironic than the original novel it adapts
the story's events change, because irony is part of what happens
questions.explanation: An ironic narrator tells readers how to view the characters, so without that voice characters may seem more sympathetic or simple unless other techniques supply the irony. The events can stay the same while their meaning shifts.

questions.stem: A novel uses an omniscient narrator who moves among many characters; its film adaptation follows only one character throughout. The adaptation most likely:
options: widens the range of perspectives well beyond those that the novel offers
keeps the same balance of viewpoints as the omniscient novel
removes any point of view, since film has no narrator at all
narrows the range of sympathies and makes the story more subjective
questions.explanation: Following one character aligns viewers with that character's experience, so other perspectives the novel explored recede. Film has no narrating voice, but framing and focus still create a point of view.

questions.stem: A novel describes a character's grief as 'a tide that would not go out'. A film adaptation is most likely to convey this metaphor through:
options: a caption on screen that reprints the novel's sentence in full
an aside in which she explains the metaphor to the audience
a screenplay scene heading such as 'EXT. BEACH – DAY'
a recurring visual motif, such as shots of the sea linked to her
questions.explanation: Film cannot film a metaphor directly, so it finds visual equivalents that viewers associate with the character's feeling. A scene heading is an instruction in the script and is never seen by the audience.

questions.stem: A play set entirely in one cramped room is filmed with scenes moved to streets, fields and other real locations. The most likely loss in meaning is:
options: the play's dialogue, which films cannot include
any connection between the characters and their context
the chronological order in which the events take place
the sense of confinement that the single setting created
questions.explanation: When a play's single space expresses entrapment, 'opening out' the action for film can dissolve that pressure. Film can keep dialogue and chronology, so those are not lost by moving locations.

questions.stem: Adapting a long novel as a television mini-series rather than a single feature film most likely allows:
options: the novel's narrator to be replaced by stage directions
the story to be told without any images or sound
the novel's setting to be moved to the present day
more subplots and gradual character development to be kept
questions.explanation: Many hours across episodes give room for the scale and slow development of a long novel, which a two-hour film must compress. Moving the setting is a separate choice that any form can make.

questions.stem: An adaptation replaces a novel's bleak ending with a hopeful reunion. This most significantly changes:
options: the text's overall view of whether people can escape their circumstances
only the final scene, leaving the text's overall meaning entirely untouched
the genre of the text from prose fiction to poetry
the setting of the text from the country to the city
questions.explanation: Endings shape how readers understand everything before them, so a hopeful close can turn a story about entrapment into one about endurance rewarded. Changing an ending is never only a local change.

questions.stem: A graphic novel adaptation of a prose novel can show a character's unspoken thoughts most directly through:
options: the splash pages
the panel borders
thought bubbles or caption boxes
the gutters between the panels
questions.explanation: Caption boxes can carry a narrating voice and thought bubbles a character's inner speech, so graphic novels keep some of prose's access to thought. The gutter is where readers infer action between panels.

questions.stem: In an analytical response comparing a text and its adaptation, the approach the study design favours is to:
options: summarise the plot of both texts first, then give a personal preference at the end
interweave both texts in each paragraph, foregrounding similarities and differences
discuss the original fully in the first half, then the adaptation fully in the second
discuss only the adaptation, since the original has already been analysed in class
questions.explanation: Interweaving keeps comparison at the centre of the analysis, so each point shows how meaning differs across the two texts. Treating the texts in separate halves leaves comparison to the reader.

questions.stem: Which sentence from a student's response best compares an original text with its adaptation?
options: The novel has a narrator who mocks the hero. The film also has a hero, and it was released many years later.
The film is much better than the novel because it is shorter and the actors bring the characters to life.
The novel is about a hero, and the film is also about a hero, which shows the adaptation is faithful.
Where the novel's narrator mocks the hero, the film's low angles ennoble him, inviting admiration the novel withholds.
questions.explanation: The strongest sentence links a specific feature of each form, narration and camera angle, to a difference in meaning. The others list features separately, judge by preference, or treat sameness of subject as the whole comparison.

questions.stem: A student argues that a stage adaptation 'emphasises' an idea from its source. The most convincing evidence would be:
options: the number of people who attended the production in its opening season
a review stating that the production was enjoyable, well acted and well attended overall
specific staging choices, such as lighting or blocking, that draw attention to that idea
the fact that the adaptation has a different title from the source text
questions.explanation: Claims about what an adaptation does must be supported by its specific choices, just as claims about a novel need quotations. Attendance figures and general praise say nothing about which ideas the production foregrounds.

questions.stem: A novel ends ambiguously, leaving it unclear whether its heroine survives. The film adaptation shows her clearly alive. A comparative analysis would most usefully argue that the film:
options: resolves an uncertainty the novel deliberately sustains, changing how its ideas land
is unfaithful, and so has nothing at all worthwhile to say about the original novel
reveals what the novelist secretly intended the novel's ending to be
proves that the novel's ending was a mistake that needed to be corrected
questions.explanation: The comparison should interpret the change: removing ambiguity may, for instance, swap the novel's unsettling openness for reassurance. A film cannot reveal a novelist's intentions, and calling it unfaithful ends the analysis rather than starting it.

questions.stem: In theatre, 'blocking' refers to:
options: the planned movements and positions of actors on the stage
the lines an actor speaks directly to the audience alone
the set pieces that hide the wings from the audience's view
the order in which the scenes of a play are performed
questions.explanation: Blocking decides where actors stand and move, which shapes relationships and focus in a scene. Lines spoken alone to the audience are a soliloquy or direct address.

questions.stem: In film, 'diegetic' sound is:
options: music added to the soundtrack that the characters themselves cannot hear
a narrator's voice heard over the images but not part of the action
the silence that the editor leaves between two separate scenes
sound that exists in the story world, such as dialogue or a radio playing in the scene
questions.explanation: Diegetic sound can be heard by the characters because it belongs to their world. A narrator's voice-over and a film score are non-diegetic, added from outside the story world.
